docs.title: The Sum Function in C++
docs.text:
Author(s):

(RGB) Raghav B. Venkataramaiyer <bv.raghav -at- thapar -dot- edu>

This project creates a sum function in c++ as a sample to illustrate how to compile a shared library and distribute it for use along with the binary.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
make -C code

This will create create a folder dist in code folder, with following contents

dist
 +-lib
 |  \-libbvr_math.so
 +-bin
    \-run

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cd code
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=dist/lib
./dist/bin/run

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My primary contribution to the BloodLine project focused on the predictive demand and shortage-analysis pipeline.

The work included:

  • Forecast model selection
  • Shortfall calculation
  • LOW/MODERATE/HIGH shortage-risk classification
  • Integration of forecasting and risk results with the BloodLine application

  • Unit expiry tracking and the multi-bank regional view
  • Role-based dashboard interface, Evaluation page and what-if scenarios
  • Login rate limiting
  • CI workflow and repository setup

docs.title: Week 12: Completing the Backend, Extending the Forecasting and Redesigning the Interface
Objective
docs.text: To audit the working prototype against the SRS, complete the missing mandatory requirements, strengthen the forecasting evaluation, and replace the basic interface with a polished role-based one.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Audited the prototype against the SRS and listed the missing requirements.
  • Implemented donation recording (FR-INV-5): a donation is accepted only after medical staff screen the donor as eligible and the cooldown has passed; it updates the last donation date and increases stock.
  • Added administrator account management (create, deactivate, change role) and an activity log of logins, stock changes and admin actions (FR-ADM-1, FR-ADM-2).
  • Added donor self-registration (FR-AUTH-4) and in-app donor notifications sent only to donors who pass the matching rules (FR-NOTE-1).
  • Extended the forecasting pipeline: added RMSE next to MAE and a SARIMA model as a third candidate. All models are compared on the same chronological, leakage-free backtest and the lowest-MAE model is selected.
  • Added unit-level expiry tracking (FR-INV-6), a multi-bank regional stock and risk view with redistribution suggestions that always need human approval (FR-REG-1), CSV/PDF report export, database migrations, Docker Compose and a CI workflow.
  • Fixed three defects found during review: an alert was stored on every dashboard load, a screening result overwrote the donor's last donation date, and first-time donors were shown as "999 days since last donation".
  • Replaced the interface with a role-based dashboard: dark and light themes, liquid blood-group tiles, gauges, donut and interactive charts, a donor picker for demo logins and a notification bell.
  • Ran the application locally and tested the main flows for each role.

docs.text: Backend unit tests were written for the risk rule (including the SRS example of 20 units in stock and 25 forecast giving MODERATE), donor matching, forecasting evaluation and the API workflows. Each role was tried manually in Chrome.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To generate realistic synthetic blood-demand data for developing and testing the forecasting module.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Detailed real-world blood-bank demand data was not available for the prototype. Therefore, synthetic data was required to simulate historical blood demand.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Implemented synthetic demand generation.
  • Generated 180 days of historical demand.
  • Generated demand for all eight blood groups.
  • Defined different baseline demand levels for each blood group.
  • Added weekly demand patterns.
  • Added seasonal variation.
  • Added holiday/event effects.
  • Added rare emergency spikes.
  • Added random noise to make the data more realistic.
  • Ensured that generated demand values remain non-negative.

docs.title: Demand Model
docs.text:
The generated demand is based on multiple components:

```text Demand = Baseline + Weekly Pattern + Seasonal Effect + Holiday Bump + Emergency Spike + Random Noise

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To implement short-term blood-demand forecasting using simple and interpretable forecasting techniques.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Studied time-series demand forecasting.
  • Implemented a 14-day baseline forecasting method.
  • Implemented Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES).
  • Used an alpha value of 0.3 for SES.
  • Generated forecasts for the next 7 days.
  • Integrated the forecasting logic into the backend service.

docs.title: 14-Day Baseline
docs.text:
The baseline uses the recent 14 days of observed demand to estimate the current daily demand level.

Baseline = Average demand over the last 14 days

The 14-day period is the historical look-back window, while the 7-day period is the future forecast horizon.

docs.title: Simple Exponential Smoothing
docs.text:
SES gives more importance to recent observations while gradually reducing the influence of older observations.

The smoothing equation is:

L_t = αX_t + (1 - α)L_(t-1)

where:

α = 0.3

docs.title: Forecast Horizon
docs.text: The system generates a short-term forecast for the next 7 days.

docs.title: Key Learning
docs.text:
The historical look-back period and forecast horizon have different purposes:

  • 14 days → data used to estimate the current demand level
  • 7 days → period for which demand is predicted

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The demand forecasting component was implemented and connected to the BloodLine backend.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To evaluate the forecasting approaches and select the better-performing model using historical data.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A forecasting model should be evaluated before being used for future predictions. Since actual future demand is not available at the time of forecasting, historical data was used for backtesting.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Implemented rolling-origin backtesting.
  • Evaluated both the baseline and SES forecasting approaches.
  • Used Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as the evaluation metric.
  • Compared predicted historical demand with actual historical demand.
  • Calculated the error for different forecasting origins.
  • Compared the average MAE of the candidate models.
  • Selected the model with the lower MAE.

docs.title: Backtesting Process
docs.text: Historical Demand ↓ Select a historical forecast origin ↓ Generate forecast using only previous data ↓ Compare forecast with actual demand ↓ Calculate MAE ↓ Move the forecast origin forward ↓ Repeat

docs.title: MAE
docs.text:
Mean Absolute Error is calculated as:

MAE = Mean(|Actual - Predicted|)

A lower MAE indicates that the forecasting method produced smaller prediction errors.

docs.title: Model Selection
docs.text: The baseline and SES models were evaluated using the same historical data. The model producing the lower MAE was selected for the final forecast.

docs.title: Key Learning
docs.text: The actual future demand cannot be compared with today's prediction immediately because the future values are not yet known. Backtesting solves this problem by using known historical data to simulate future predictions.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The forecasting pipeline was enhanced with objective evaluation and model selection instead of relying on a single forecasting method without validation.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To determine whether the predicted blood demand can be met using the current inventory and classify the shortage risk.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Implemented shortage-risk detection.
  • Used forecasted demand and current stock as inputs.
  • Calculated the expected shortfall.
  • Implemented LOW, MODERATE, and HIGH risk levels.
  • Added special handling for zero-stock situations.
  • Generated explanations for the assigned risk level.

docs.title: Shortfall Calculation
docs.text:
The expected shortage is calculated as:

Shortfall = Predicted Demand - Current Stock

For example:

Predicted demand = 83.4 units Current stock = 10 units

Shortfall = 83.4 - 10 = 73.4 units

docs.title: LOW
docs.text:
Shortfall ≤ 0

The current stock is sufficient to cover the predicted demand.

docs.title: MODERATE
docs.text:
0 < Shortfall ≤ 25% of current stock

There is a shortage, but it remains within the defined moderate threshold.

docs.title: HIGH
docs.text:
Shortfall > 25% of current stock

A zero-stock situation with positive predicted demand is also treated as HIGH risk.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Current stock = 10 7-day forecast = 83.4

Shortfall = 83.4 - 10 = 73.4

Since the shortfall is greater than the defined threshold, the blood group is classified as HIGH risk.

docs.title: Key Learning
docs.text: Forecasting tells us how much blood may be required, while shortage-risk detection determines whether the current inventory is sufficient to satisfy that predicted demand.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: A rule-based shortage-risk detection layer was implemented on top of the forecasting output, producing interpretable LOW, MODERATE, and HIGH risk levels.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To integrate the forecasting and shortage-risk components with the BloodLine application and verify their complete workflow.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Integrated the forecasting service with the BloodLine backend.
  • Integrated shortage-risk calculations with the application.
  • Connected forecasting and risk results with the dashboard.
  • Verified that forecasted demand and shortage-risk levels are displayed for blood groups.
  • Tested different inventory and demand scenarios.

  • Tested the complete flow from historical demand to forecast and risk detection.
  • Verified that high-risk results can lead to the donor-matching workflow.

docs.title: End-to-End Workflow
docs.text: Historical Demand ↓ Demand Forecasting ↓ Baseline / SES Evaluation ↓ Selected Forecast ↓ Compare Forecast with Current Stock ↓ Shortfall Calculation ↓ Risk Classification ↓ LOW / MODERATE / HIGH ↓ Dashboard / Risk Alert ↓ Potential Donor Matching

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The predictive workflow was tested using different combinations of:

  • Blood groups
  • Current inventory levels
  • Forecasted demand
  • Shortage conditions
  • Zero-stock situations

The results were checked to ensure that the calculated risk level matched the defined rules.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The demand forecasting and shortage-risk components were integrated into the working BloodLine prototype and verified as part of the complete application workflow.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To study which time-series models suit blood-demand data better than the baseline and Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) built earlier, and to plan how they would be compared.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Reviewed the limits of the baseline and SES models: both forecast a flat level, so they cannot represent the weekly pattern in daily demand.
  • Studied SARIMA (seasonal ARIMA) and Prophet as the two options named in the proposal, including what the order terms (p, d, q) and the seasonal terms mean and why a seven-day season fits daily demand.
  • Compared the options on practical grounds: data needed, ease of fitting, interpretability, dependencies and how well each can be evaluated fairly against the existing models.
  • Planned the evaluation protocol: a chronological train/test split, no use of future data when forecasting, MAE and RMSE as the metrics, and the moving-average baseline as the reference every model must beat.
  • Outlined how the model would be kept replaceable, so a new model can be added without changing the API.
  • [Add any sources, notes or discussions with teammates here.]

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: A clear plan: add SARIMA as a third candidate next to the baseline and SES, and compare all three on the same chronological backtest.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To document the complete requirements of the BloodLine platform in a Software Requirements Specification so that design, implementation and testing can be checked against it.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Contributed to the SRS (version 1.0) for BloodLine with the team. [State your part, for example the forecasting, shortage-risk and donor-matching sections.]
  • Described the six user classes (donors, hospital coordinators, inventory staff, blood-bank manager, medical staff, system administrator) and what each role may do.
  • Wrote numbered functional requirements grouped by feature: authentication (FR-AUTH), inventory (FR-INV), demand forecasting (FR-FCST), shortage risk (FR-RISK), donor matching (FR-MATCH), requests, screening, notifications, reports and regional view, donor portal and administration.
  • Specified the shortage-risk rule: shortfall = forecast demand - current stock; LOW if shortfall <= 0, MODERATE up to 25% of stock, HIGH above 25% or when stock is zero and demand is expected.
  • Specified the donor-compatibility table and the matching rules (compatible group, availability, consent, cooldown period).
  • Defined the data model (users, donors, blood banks, inventory, transactions, demand history, predictions, alerts, requests, screening records).
  • Added non-functional requirements (inventory update within 1 s, dashboard within 3 s and donor search within 2 s for up to 50 users), security requirements and business rules, such as final donor clearance by medical staff only and simulated data never being presented as real.

docs.title: Outcome
